newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek seamen's strike cuts off Aegean islands.
newsitem.headline: Greek seamen's strike cuts off Aegean islands.

text.p: A Greek seamen's strike crippled sea transport for a 10th day on Wednesday, cutting off remote islands and stranding lorries with tonnes of rotting farm produce at docks.
Problems in Greek transport are expected to worsen on Thursday, when Greece's biggest labour confederation, GSEE, stages a 24-hour nationwide walkout against a new tax system.

"Our society cannot be turned into a jungle," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters. "We call on workers (and seamen) to show restraint and respect, and to deal with the increasing problems they have created."
The socialist government elected in September successfully waited out a farmers' road blockade in December but is facing a new wave of labour unrest over its tough economic policies.
The seamen's strike has left scores of trucks lined up waiting for ferries to sail, while Greek islands dependent on ships for survival have reported shortages in food and supplies.
"There are shortages in food, supplies, fuel and animal feed," Aegean Minister Elisavet Papazoi told reporters. "The situation is borderline."
Ministry officials said bad weather has been hindering efforts to get supplies to remore Aegean islands with small private boats, navy ships and airplanes.

The GSEE walkout is expected to further disrupt transport on Thursday, with trains and buses on strike for the day and the national carrier Olympic airways staging a three-hour work stoppage between 1000 and 1300 GMT, GSEE said in a statement.

Labour groups are reacting to Greece's tough 1997 budget and tight incomes and tax policies but Prime Minister Costas Simitis has adamantly rejected all demands, saying the country needs bitter medicine to turn its ailing economy around.

State hospitals, public services and several state companies will be forced to operate with skeleton staff on Thursday while high school teachers have been on an indefinite strike since Monday to push for better pay.

The Panhellenic Seamen's Federation (PNO) defied a court ruling declaring their walkout illegal and vowed to push on until demands for better pensions, tax status and measures against unemployment are met.
"We plan to continue the strike because no solution has been found. Unemployment in our sector reaches 40 percent," PNO representative Aristides Koletsis told Reuters.
The strike affects all ships with Greek crews and has kept most vessels idle at ports around the country.

Scuffles have broken out between seamen, angry farmers and truck drivers at the ports of Piraeus, the Peloponnese and on the island of Crete. Special coast guard forces have intervened to keep them apart.

Exporters on the island of Crete said damage to the island's economy had reached $68 million and was rising. The defence ministry has sent air carriers and navy vessels to Crete to transport perishables destined for export.
Farmers have also threatened to repeat their paralysing road blockade if they get no government pledges by February 4 that their demands for higher price supports, fuel and tax cuts will be met.
